Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I can't deal with even the slightest upset
The event happened because of the way I acted

vignette: Anna Kowalski, a 26-year-old firefighter, had always prided herself on being the calmest presence in any emergency. That changed after the night she was held captive by a man with a shotgun during what should have been a routine welfare check. She had entered the apartment first, the rest of her crew still on the stairs. The door slammed behind her. For four hours she lay face-down on a filthy carpet, listening to him rant, her helmet digging into her cheek, until negotiators talked him down. In those hours, running through every choice that had brought her to that hallway, she became certain she should have waited—she had acted impulsively, and that decision had nearly killed her. Weeks later, Anna found herself scanning every face on every call for a threat. Old family photos she had once kept on her phone began to feel unbearable; glancing at an image of herself from before the incident made the memory of the carpet and the shotgun appear in her mind as if it were happening again, the photographic clarity leaving her breathless. Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light. The memory itself felt alien—it belonged to someone else, someone who had been helpless—yet it was more real than any ordinary day, and this contrast made her suspect she had lost the person she used to be. She began to blame herself more: if she had been smarter, quicker, the event would not have happened, and that self-blame made the image return with even greater force, as if punishing her. Her sense of low coping deepened: she could no longer handle even a minor upset at the station, and because she believed she could not cope, her body stayed locked in a state of alert, her heart hammering at the sound of a dropped hose or a closed door. Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been. That constant startle response, in turn, sometimes tripped a full flashback—she would feel as if she were back on the carpet, and the terror of that moment would trigger the same intrusive memory again, tightening the loop. Crowded spaces, which she had once navigated easily on a packed ambulance, now felt suffocating. The pressure of bodies told her, with a quiet certainty, that she had become someone who could not be trusted to handle ordinary situations. The pressure of bodies reminded her of the weight of the shotgun barrel, and that trigger would instantly activate the memory—the smell of the carpet, the man's voice—and the memory would then reinforce her appraisal that she was fundamentally changed, broken in a way that made her unfit for the job. At the firehouse, she began eating alone, sitting in the truck bay where no one could crowd her, because the social bustle of the kitchen triggered the same sense of entrapment. This avoidance made her feel even more alien to herself: who was this person who could not stand beside her crew? That identity loss fed her inability to relax; even in the quiet of her own apartment, she found herself listening for footsteps, certain she was not safe, and that hypervigilance made the memory more vivid, as if the event had etched itself into her senses and would not fade. The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair. Her inability to relax meant she rarely slept. The exhaustion compounded her low coping, and the low coping made her more sensitive to triggers—she would avoid looking at her phone because a notification sound could send her back into the memory. She came to believe that the memory was not just a story from her past but an active threat, and this belief kept her scanning, kept her tensed, kept the memory ready to surface at any moment. Her relationships with her colleagues suffered; they noticed she was jumpy and withdrawn, but she could not explain why she could no longer sit in the backseat of the engine without feeling the walls close in. It was after a shift in which she had yanked open a door and immediately dropped into a protective crouch, earning confused looks, that Anna finally called a therapist. What frightened her most was the thought that she might never feel like herself again—that the captivity had stripped away the person who had loved the job, and that she would spend the rest of her life flinching at ordinary sounds and seeing that shotgun barrel in her mind's eye. She came hoping, quietly, that someone could help her understand why the memory felt so real and so alien at once, and whether she could ever trust herself to walk into a room first again. After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore.

violations.explanation: No paragraph shows that a trigger directly leads to a negative appraisal; triggers lead to memory, which then leads to appraisals, but the direct causal link from trigger to appraisal is absent.
No paragraph shows that the intrusive memory directly causes or increases triggers; instead, triggers activate the memory.
No paragraph shows that sense of threat directly leads to negative appraisals; threat often leads to memory or hypervigilance, but not to appraisals.
No paragraph shows that sense of threat directly leads to the creation or increase of triggers; threat amplifies responses to triggers but does not cause triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph shows that a trigger directly leads to a negative appraisal; triggers lead to memory, which then leads to appraisals, but the direct causal link from trigger to appraisal is absent.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph shows that the intrusive memory directly causes or increases triggers; instead, triggers activate the memory.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph shows that sense of threat directly leads to negative appraisals; threat often leads to memory or hypervigilance, but not to appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph shows that sense of threat directly leads to the creation or increase of triggers; threat amplifies responses to triggers but does not cause triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
